articles.title: Last chance: 8 Amazon gadgets hit their lowest prices ever for Prime Day
articles.description: October Prime Day ends today, which means this is your last opportunity to grab Amazon’s marked-down products, including Blink, Ring, Echo, Fire TV, and Eero devices. Not sure which ones are worth pulling the trigger on? I’ll guide you to the best discounts going on right now. I didn’t just go through Amazon’s search results and pluck out what look like good deals. Every product on this list fits two criteria: it’s at a significant discount compared to its “street price,” and I would actually buy this product at this price over same-class items from other brands. If I wouldn’t seriously consider it for my own cart, it doesn’t qualify for this list. Prime caveat: While some of these deals can be had without an active Prime subscription, others can’t. But don’t fret if you don’t have Prime. See our article on how to get Amazon Prime for free to score the following discounts—and others—without paying for a sub. Deals at a glance Blink Outdoor 4 Cam and Battery Doorbell 2K+ (Bundle) for $65.99 (lowest price ever — 75% off, was $259.98) Ring Indoor Cam for $24.99 (lowest price ever — 50% off, was $49.99) Ember 4K Smart TV (55-Inch) for $279.99 (lowest price ever — 39% off, was $459.99) Luna Wireless Gaming Controller for $39.99 (lowest price ever — 43% off, was $69.99) Fire TV Stick 4K Plus for $37.99 (46% off, was $69.99) Fire TV Cube for $89.99 (lowest price ever — 55% off, was $199.99) Fire TV Soundbar for $79.99 (lowest price ever — 33% off, was $119.99) Fire HD 10 Tablet for $72.99 (lowest price ever — 53% off, was $154.99) Echo Show 11 for $149.99 (lowest price ever — 40% off, was $249.99) Eero 6+ Mesh Wi-Fi System (3-Pack) for $214.99 (28% off, was $299.99) Blink Outdoor 4 Cam and Battery Doorbell 2K+ (Bundle) Blink Now $65.99 (lowest price ever — 75% off, was $259.98) You could get the Blink Outdoor 4 for $65.99, which is already a solid discount off its usual $99.99… or you could get this Blink Outdoor 4 + Blink Battery Doorbell 2K+ bundle for the exact same price. Do I need to spell it out for you? This bundle effectively gives you a free Battery Doorbell 2K+, allowing you to watch your doorstep and your backyard with these two outdoor cameras. Check in on your feeds via the Blink app on your phone and you’ll always have peace of mind—even while on vacation. Get this Blink Bundle at Amazon Ring Indoor Cam Ring Now $24.99 (lowest price ever — 50% off, was $49.99) The Ring Indoor Cam gives you vantage over any room in your house. Mount it on top of a table, or screw it higher up into a wall—its swivel design lets you point it at wherever you want it looking over. It’s pretty basic with 1080p resolution, but it has color night vision and a live feed that you can tune into via the Ring app on your phone. If all you need is straightforward interior surveillance at home, this one’s a solid pick at $24.99. Get the Ring Indoor Cam at Amazon Ember 4K Smart TV (55-Inch) Amazon Now $279.99 (lowest price ever — 39% off, was $459.99) Yup, Amazon makes its own line of big smart TVs. This Ember 4-Series has a 55-inch diagonal, perfect for living rooms and spacious bedrooms, and it comes with an Alexa Remote for convenient control. 4K resolution, HDR10+ support, and Dolby Audio for just $279.99 make it a strong budget-friendly pick if you’re mainly streaming shows and films in 4K. It also has something called Ambient Experience, which displays artwork or a smart interactive hub when in standby mode (and only when it detects people nearby). Get the 55-inch Ember 4K TV at Amazon Luna Wireless Gaming Controller Amazon Now $39.99 (lowest price ever — 43% off, was $69.99) Though it was designed for use with Amazon’s Luna cloud gaming platform, the Luna controller works with anything. Connect it via Bluetooth to your PC, gaming console, or even your phone. It also supports USB wired, but only with Windows and macOS devices. Neither budget nor premium, it’s a good middle-of-the-road option with a comfortable, standard layout (offset thumbsticks), bumpers, triggers, and a directional pad. At $39.99, it’s a step up from most other wireless controllers in this range. Get the Luna Gaming Controller at Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus Amazon Now $37.99 (46% off, was $69.99) Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is great for two reasons. It plugs into any device that supports HDMI input (e.g., TVs, monitors, projectors) and lets you stream from dozens of services like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime Video. But your accounts are logged on the stick itself, so if you take it with you to a hotel, Airbnb, or friend’s house, you just plug in and resume your shows and movies from wherever you left off. The 4K Plus is the balanced option in Amazon’s Fire TV Stick lineup. While the 4K Select is cheaper, it runs on a different OS that’s slower and doesn’t allow for sideloading apps. Meanwhile, the more expensive 4K Max is faster and has twice the storage. If you’re only going to be streaming shows and movies—meaning you won’t be downloading many apps, games, or files—then the 4K Plus is the way to go. Get the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus at Amazon Fire TV Cube Amazon Now $89.99 (lowest price ever — 55% off, was $199.99) Whereas the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is more than fine for basic streaming, the Fire TV Cube is what you want if you have a decked-out home media setup. The Cube is much faster with its upgraded octa-core processor and extra RAM, so apps launch more quickly, navigation is more responsive, and gaming performance feels better. It has Super Resolution, which upscales HD content so it looks better on 4K displays. If you’re going to cloud-stream Xbox games or if on-screen lag really bothers you, get the Cube. Get the Fire TV Cube at Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Amazon Now $79.99 (lowest price ever — 33% off, was $119.99) No matter how much you spend on a TV, the built-in speakers are almost guaranteed to suck—and there’s no easier upgrade than to add in a soundbar. You don’t have to spend a lot either. At $79.99, Amazon’s Fire TV Soundbar is as good as it gets in this price range, punching up bass for a fuller experience while improving voice clarity so you can actually understand what characters are saying on screen. Amazon also has a stepped-up model called the Fire TV Soundbar Plus . Whereas the regular Soundbar is 24 inches, the Soundbar Plus is 37 inches—a better acoustic and aesthetic fit for larger TVs (55-inch and bigger). It can also pair with a wireless subwoofer and satellite speakers for true surround sound. If that’s important to you, you’ll want the Soundbar Plus instead. Get the Fire TV Soundbar at Amazon Get the Fire TV Soundbar Plus at Amazon Fire HD 10 Tablet Amazon Now $72.99 (lowest price ever — 53% off, was $154.99) Amazon sells several tablet models, with the most popular ones being the Fire HD 10 and Fire HD 8. I have the Fire HD 8 and I regret it, mainly because it’s too sluggish for anything but extremely basic uses. The Fire HD 10 is what I now recommend for a budget tablet. It has a faster octa-core processor and extra RAM, resulting in better responsiveness that doesn’t slow you down. The larger 10.1-inch display is the cherry on top. Get the Fire HD 10 Tablet at Amazon Echo Show 11 Amazon Now $149.99 (lowest price ever — 40% off, was $249.99) If you’re going to get an Echo in 2026, ask yourself: How deep into the Alexa ecosystem are you willing to go? If you think you’ll ever add more Alexa-compatible gadgets to your home—like any of the other stuff on this list—then you’ll want the Echo Show 11 . At first glance, it just looks like a tablet-plus-speaker; it’s actually a smart home hub that makes it easy to control various smart home devices. Sure, you can play music and browse the web on it, but it shines as a central command for controlling your smart thermostat, viewing your camera feeds, changing your smart lights, locking your door, playing media on your TV, and more. Today’s the day to grab one now that it’s at its lowest price. Get the Echo Show 11 at Amazon Eero 6+ Mesh Wi-Fi System Amazon Now $214.99 (28% off, was $299.99) If you live in a large home—I’m talking 2,000+ square feet—then you’ve probably run into spotty Wi-Fi. Maybe your connection drops while walking around, or certain rooms get terrible signal. If so, you’d benefit from a mesh Wi-Fi system. Unlike a traditional router, mesh Wi-Fi uses multiple “nodes” around the home to expand and strengthen coverage. The Eero 6+ Mesh Wi-Fi System is what most households need. It supports up to 1Gbps internet plans, and it supports Wi-Fi 6 with wider 160MHz channels (faster and more reliable than standard 80MHz channels). You should only consider the newer Eero 7 system if you’re paying for a multi-gigabit internet plan, as it goes up to 2.5Gbps, or if you have 100+ smart devices congesting your network. If neither apply, you’re better off saving money with the Eero 6+ instead. Get the Eero 6+ Mesh Wi-Fi System at Amazon Get the Eero 7 Mesh Wi-Fi System at Amazon

articles.title: Cisco brings collaborative agents and Claude into Webex chats
articles.description: Cisco is adding AI agents to Webex group chats so colleagues can assign them work and share the results, part of a wider revamp of the Webex app. Announced at the WebexOne conference Wednesday, users will soon be able to @mention agents in Webex “spaces” to help schedule meetings, take notes, and track tasks. “You work with AI, but your teammates may never see that work — they can’t build on it, contribute to it, or reuse it,” said Amit Barave, Cisco vice president and general manager for Webex Suite and AI, in a blog post . “With Webex, agents become part of the team, participating where the work is happening.” “This makes AI a shared capability for the team,” said Snorre Kjesbu, Cisco vice president and general manager for collaboration, in a separate blog post . “It can help people prepare together, carry decisions forward, and coordinate the next steps without losing the context of the conversation.” As well as Webex spaces, the collaborative agents will be accessible during video and voice calls via the AI Assistant side panel, though these will only be visible to individual users, rather than teams, a Cisco spokesperson said. Cisco’s announcement reflects the growing push from collaboration software vendors to bring AI agents directly into their applications, said Irwin Lazar, principal analyst at Metrigy. By positioning agents where employees are already collaborating, they are able to perform tasks such as managing meeting agendas, facilitating, and providing contextual information into meetings. “We’ve seen similar efforts by Slack, with Claude Tag , and with Zoom via ZoomMate,” said Lazar. “Like the others, the strength of the agent is dependent on its access to information, so the key is enabling connectivity to external data sources such as CRM, ERP, project management, etc.” The changes are part of a wider Webex app refresh app that includes a new personalized landing page to highlight work priorities and upcoming meetings, as well as suggest follow-up actions, such as responding to messages or reviewing meeting recaps. “The new assistant literally knows what you are doing and your upcoming schedule and knows more than other major providers,” said Jim Lundy, CEO of Aragon Research. “In fact, I’d say that their assistant could be sold unbundled.” width="1024" height="657" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px"> Cisco In addition, Cisco is extending the range of third-party agents accessible from Webex, too. Anthropic’s Claude Managed Agents — cloud-hosted agents that process multi-step tasks in the background — can be added to group conversations as a team member to complete tasks, as well as OpenAI’s recently announced “dot” agents. Cisco also unveiled more of its own native Webex agents. Personal Agents for Webex Calling can screen calls to help users avoid missing an important call when they’re unavailable to speak. The agents can “converse with callers to understand their needs and determine urgency, prioritize what matters most, and take action on your behalf,” Barava said. Personal Agents for Webex Calling will be available in the first quarter of 2027, alongside the new Webex app, collaborative agents, third-party agents. A previously announced Translator agent is now in “controlled availability” ahead of a general release in November. This provides real-time translation in the Webex app, as well as Cisco 9800 Series Desk Phones, with support for ten languages: English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, Portuguese, and Spanish. An AI Coach agent for Vidcast — Cisco’s tool for short form, asynchronous video messaging in Webex — is aimed at helping users improve communication performance. “The AI Coach watches and listens while a presenter delivers, reacts to pacing, tone, and word choice as they happen, and asks the questions a live audience would,” said Barave. The AI Coach agent is available now. Metrigy’s Lazar said he has witnessed an uptick in business demand for agentic tools in collaboration applications generally. “They offer the potential to bring context into meetings, saving time and increasing focus. Cisco’s aim is to ensure that the Webex App can remain the place where people work, rather than other apps or AI interfaces like Claude Cowork,” he said. “I would say the only weakness in the Cisco portfolio now is ability to capture data from non-Webex meetings. They lack the capability that Zoom now has to capture audio from third-party or external meetings.” A Cisco spokesperson said that some Webex AI capabilities are available at no extra cost in Webex Suite, which costs $25 per user each month, and Enterprise tiers. More advanced features — such as Polling and Translator agents, the Personal Agents for Calling, and collaborative agent functionality — will require a new “Enhanced AI Offer for AI” add-on. This will be available in the coming weeks, Cisco said, though pricing for the add-on was not provided. Cisco didn’t specify if any of the AI features will require any additional, usage-based costs on top of fixed subscription fees. The company recently stated that the Translator agent provides 50 minutes of translation per user each month, with additional usage requiring an “add-on.”
